subject: microbiology
title: L-Forms, Bacterial Growth Curve and Culture Physiology

steps.tx: **L-forms** are bacteria that have lost their cell wall wholly or partly, named for the Lister Institute where Klieneberger described them in 1935: protoplasts (gram positive, wall fully lost), spheroplasts (gram negative, wall remnants) and stable L forms that grow without walls on osmotically protective media in fried egg colonies. Wall active antibiotics can induce them, and their clinical reality in persistent infection remains debated rather than established.
steps.say: Strip the wall and the bacterium survives as a fragile sphere, if the medium protects it osmotically.

left.title: Wall deficient forms
points: Protoplast: gram positive wall completely lost
Spheroplast: gram negative partial wall retained
Unstable forms revert when inducer removed
Stable L forms propagate without walls

right.title: Recognition
points: Fried egg colonies on hypertonic media
Induced by penicillin and lysozyme in vitro
Mycoplasma is a natural wall less genus, not an L form

steps.tx: **L forms** are bacteria that have lost the cell wall completely or in part. They were named for the Lister Institute, where Klieneberger described them in 1935. Protoplasts are gram positive cells with the wall fully gone. Spheroplasts are gram negative cells that keep wall remnants. Stable L forms keep dividing without a wall if the medium protects them osmotically, and their colonies look like fried eggs. Antibiotics that attack the wall can induce these forms. Whether they truly sustain persistent infection in patients is still debated, not settled.
steps.say: L forms lack a complete cell wall. Klieneberger described them at the Lister Institute in 1935. Gram positive protoplasts lose the wall entirely. Gram negative spheroplasts keep scraps of it. Stable forms grow without walls on media that protect them from osmotic burst, forming fried egg colonies. Wall active antibiotics can create them. A role in persistent human infection is still unproved.

vis.alt: Wall deficient L form colonies spread with a dense centre and a thin edge on osmotically protective medium.
vis.caption: Soft colonies show a dense centre and a thin periphery, the fried egg look of L forms grown without a rigid wall. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **bacterial growth curve** in closed culture runs four acts: **lag phase** (enzymes synthesised, no division, length set by inoculum history), **log or exponential phase** (balanced doubling at generation time, organisms most uniform and antibiotic susceptible), stationary phase (nutrient exhaustion and waste, growth equals death, spores and secondary metabolites appear), and decline phase. Every culture based test reads its inoculum from log phase for reproducibility.
steps.say: Lag adapts, log doubles, stationary starves, decline dies; log phase is the laboratory's standard actor.

steps.tx: The **bacterial growth curve** in a closed culture has four phases. During lag, enzymes are made and cells do not divide, and the length depends on the history of the inoculum. During log, or exponential, growth, doubling is balanced and generation time is steady, so organisms are most uniform and most susceptible to antibiotics. In stationary phase, nutrients run out and waste accumulates, growth equals death, and spores and secondary metabolites appear. Decline follows. Tests that use culture take their inoculum from log phase so results can be repeated.
steps.say: Closed cultures pass through lag, log, stationary, and decline. Lag builds enzymes without division and depends on how the inoculum was grown. Log phase doubles at a steady generation time and is when cells are most alike and most antibiotic susceptible. Stationary phase balances growth and death as food fails. Laboratories standardise tests on log phase cells.

vis.alt: A graph plots bacterial numbers over time through lag, exponential, stationary, and decline phases in a closed culture.
vis.caption: Cell numbers stay flat, then rise steeply, level off as growth matches death, and finally fall as the closed culture fails. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Generation time** grades bacterial patience: E coli doubles in about 20 minutes in rich broth, Mycobacterium tuberculosis in 18 to 24 hours, Mycobacterium leprae in about two weeks (in mouse footpads, never yet in broth), which is why tuberculosis cultures report in weeks and leprosy in animal passages. Arithmetic follows: one E coli becomes billions overnight, explaining colony timing and food poisoning incubation scales.
steps.say: Twenty minutes versus twenty hours versus two weeks: generation time sets the laboratory calendar.

left.title: Doubling league
points: M leprae: about 12 to 14 days (in vivo)

steps.tx: **Oxygen requirements classify** bench handling: obligate aerobes (M tuberculosis, Pseudomonas), obligate anaerobes (next lesson), facultative anaerobes (most enterics, growing either way), microaerophiles (Campylobacter, Helicobacter at 5 to 10 percent oxygen) and capnophiles needing added carbon dioxide (Neisseria, pneumococcus enriched in CO2 incubators). Thioglycollate broth layers these preferences into one tube's gradient.
steps.say: Read the thioglycollate tube from top to bottom and the oxygen class announces itself.

right.title: Bench systems
points: Thioglycollate and Robertson cooked meat media
McIntosh Fildes and GasPak anaerobic jars

steps.tx: **Nutrition and environment** write culture requirements: temperature optima (mesophiles at 37 degrees, Yersinia and Listeria growing in refrigerators, Campylobacter jejuni at 42), pH tolerances (Vibrio cholerae alkaline, lactobacilli acid), salt (halophilic vibrios), and growth factors called fastidiousness (Haemophilus demanding X and V factors from the respiratory lessons). Cold enrichment and alkaline media are physiology exploited as selection.
steps.say: Every selective medium is an organism's physiology turned into a trap for its rivals.

left.title: Exploited physiologies
points: Alkaline peptone water selects Vibrio cholerae
Cold enrichment selects Listeria and Yersinia
Salt media select halophilic vibrios and staphylococci

steps.tx: **Bacterial metabolism names** the identification bench: fermentation versus oxidation of sugars, enzyme armament (catalase, coagulase, oxidase from the culture module), end products from glucose (mixed acid in E coli, butylene glycol in Klebsiella behind the IMViC pattern), and pigment and haemolysis as metabolic signatures. Biochemical panels are physiology interrogated systematically, now miniaturised into automated galleries.
steps.say: A biochemical panel is twenty physiology questions asked of one colony overnight.

right.title: Metabolic signatures
points: Pigments: Pseudomonas blue green, S aureus gold
Hydrogen sulfide in TSI agar blackening

steps.tx: **Stationary phase is** where bacteria arm for survival: endospores form, competence for DNA uptake peaks in some species (genetics module), secondary metabolites including many antibiotics are secreted (Streptomyces in soil warfare), and persister cells tolerate antibiotics phenotypically without resistance genes. Biofilm and stationary physiology together explain why chronic infections shrug at drugs that kill log phase cultures beautifully.
steps.say: Starving bacteria make spores, antibiotics and persisters; log phase susceptibility is a fair weather report.

steps.tx: **Diauxic growth** (Monod's double curve) shows regulatory economy: glucose first, then a second lag while lactose enzymes are induced (the lac operon at work), producing two log phases separated by a plateau. It is the growth curve's built in genetics lesson and the reason mixed sugar media read sequentially in fermentation tests.
steps.say: Two sugars, two growth spurts, one operon switching between them.
